title: Prompt Cartography — private deployment notes
content:
Purpose / elevator:
Quick personal thinking doc for a small feature set I want to prototype for Private customers: a lightweight ‘prompt cartography’ system that maps reusable prompt fragments and response object templates to deployment-safe modules. Goal: reduce prompt duplication across apps, make safe-by-default templates for regulated/private deployments, and surface a tiny UX for engineers to mix-and-match response modules without editing raw prompt text.

High-level idea (one-liner):
- Treat prompts as composable building blocks (instructions, safety guardrails, context adapters, persona kernels, post-process transforms) and expose a minimal authoring layer in Redwood Private that can assemble these blocks into final payloads while enforcing compliance filters and runtime routing constraints.

Why this helps (user problems):
- Private customers often copy/paste long prompt blobs into templates and then struggle to audit or update them later.
- Security/compliance teams want auditable, parameterized fragments instead of freeform text per endpoint.
- Product teams want to iterate on behavior quickly (swap a persona, tighten summarization length) without changing application code.
- Reduces per-endpoint token bloat by reusing shared modules (cacheable) and enables safer default configs in private infra.

Core concepts / data model (sketch):
- Module types (this is just thinking, keep simple):
  - instruction: core instruction text (short, canonical)
  - guardrail: safety filter / refusals / redaction hints
  - adapter: transforms input (e.g., compress, extract salient bits)
  - persona: small behavior modifiers (tone, verbosity)
  - postproc: deterministic transformations on model output (truncate, JSON-validate)
  - meta: metadata for auditing (owner, version, tags, last-updated)
- Assembly: a lightweight manifest that lists module ids + parameter overrides in ordered sequence
- Runtime contract: when assembled, the runtime performs:
  1) validation against blacklist/whitelist (private deployment policy)
  2) optional on-disk hashing to map to cached KV prompt fragment output
  3) compile into final request for selected model variant (quantized/float)

UX surface (very small MVP):
- Authoring panel (Private console): name + type + text body + quick tags + save as version
- Endpoint binding: add a reference to a manifest from route config (route can reference multiple manifests; manifests are exported as policy safe strings)
- Preview: assemble and preview token counts and compiled prompt (read-only for non-authorized users)
- Audit view: show 1-line diff between versions, owner, and approve/rollback buttons

Acceptance criteria (MVP):
- Create/edit modules (instruction, persona, guardrail, postproc) in Private console
- Assemble a manifest of up to 6 modules and attach to a Private route
- Runtime validates manifest against a per-tenant denylist AND compiles into a model request
- Token delta preview displayed in console and in route logs

User stories (examples):
- As an enterprise security lead, I want prompt guardrails to be centrally defined so app devs can’t accidentally call out PHI in prompts.
- As a product engineer, I want to swap personas between routes without code deploys so A/B testing is faster.
- As an SRE, I want assembled manifests to show predictable token usage so capacity planning is easier.

Metrics / signals to watch (early):
- % of private routes that bind to a cartography manifest (adoption)
- number of unique modules created per tenant (reuse rate)
- average token saving per compiled request vs baseline (cost impact)
- number of policy violations blocked by guardrails (safety value)
- time-to-change for behavior (from edit -> live) for product teams

Rollout / experiment plan (very rough):
- Phase 0 (internal dogfood): console-only in Redwood staging, 2 internal apps bind manifests, get signal on token previews and authoring UX (2 weeks)
- Phase 1 (Opt-in private alpha): invite 3 enterprise customers with small integrations; enable audit log retention and denylist enforcement (6 weeks)
- Phase 2 (public Private): documentation + examples + migration guide for teams with existing monolithic prompts (8 weeks)

Quick tech notes / constraints:
- Avoid building a full DSL for now. Use simple parameter substitution + ordering semantics.
- Modules should be small text blobs (max 2k chars) to keep edit/preview simple.
- Store as tenant-scoped resources in control plane DB with hashed snapshots for runtime lookup.
- Runtime should compile server-side; avoid client-side assembly for Private to preserve auditability.

Open questions / risks (brain dump):
- Policy model: how strict should guardrails be? block vs annotate? need approvals UX for exceptions.
- Compatibility with streaming: assembled prompt may need chunked streaming; ensure postproc modules don’t break stream logic.
- Caching: need to find a stable cache key strategy that accounts for model variant + manifest version + tenant policy.
- Migration UX: how to help customers convert long static prompts to modules without manual copy/paste? maybe a simple "extractors" tool.

Immediate TODOs (next 7 days):
- mockup console authoring wireframe (low-fi) — Mika
- stub JIRA tickets for backend storage + compile endpoint — me
- run quick token-cost sim with existing internal prompts to estimate saving opportunities — Arjun

Notes to self: keep scope tight — this is a developer ergonomics feature first, not a governance overhaul. Prioritize quick wins (token preview, binding manifest to route) and let guardrails iterate after initial user feedback.

Random links / references I should read before next sync:
- Confluence: prompt modularity patterns (linked above)
- internal thread: #private-onboard (Slack) about compliance automation
- prior notes: "prompt-provenance-lineage-idea-log.json" (drive)

End of notes.
